questions.stem: In sensation, the process of converting physical energy such as light into electrochemical neural impulses is called:
questions.explanation: Transduction is the conversion of stimulus energy into neural impulses by sensory receptors. Transmission is the next step, when those impulses travel along neural pathways to the brain.

questions.stem: Light reaches the photoreceptors of the retina, is converted into neural impulses, and the impulses travel along the optic nerve to the occipital lobe. The final step described is:
questions.explanation: Transmission is the sending of neural impulses from the receptors to the relevant area of the brain. Transduction happened earlier, at the photoreceptors, when light energy was converted into impulses.

questions.stem: At a noisy party, Mia notices her own name spoken across the room while ignoring other conversations. Which process of perception does this mainly show?
questions.explanation: Selection is the process of attending to some sensory information while filtering out the rest. Organisation and interpretation follow, when the selected information is arranged and given meaning.

questions.stem: How does sensation differ from perception?
options: Sensation is learned through experience; perception is entirely innate
Sensation detects and transmits stimuli; perception gives them meaning
Perception detects stimuli; sensation organises and interprets them
Sensation happens in the brain; perception happens only in the receptors
questions.explanation: Sensation is the detection of stimuli by receptors and the transmission of that information to the brain. Perception is the brain's selection, organisation and interpretation of it, so it is shaped by experience and expectations.

questions.stem: Two students see the same ambiguous shape. One, a keen birdwatcher, reports a bird; the other, a sailor, reports a boat. The difference is best explained by individual differences in:
options: transmission, based on the speed of neural impulses
reception, based on the number of receptors
transduction, based on the strength of the stimulus
questions.explanation: Both students receive and transduce the same image, so the sensory processes are the same. Interpretation gives meaning to the organised information using past experience, which is why each person sees something familiar.

questions.stem: The memory process of converting information into a usable form so that it can be stored is called:
questions.explanation: Encoding converts information into a form the memory system can use and store. Storage is retaining it over time, and retrieval is bringing it back into conscious awareness.

questions.stem: During an exam, Tom remembers the definition of a term that he learned two weeks earlier. Which memory process is he using?
questions.explanation: Retrieval is locating stored information and bringing it back into conscious awareness when it is needed. Encoding and storage happened two weeks earlier, when he learned and retained the definition.

questions.stem: In the multi-store model of memory (Atkinson and Shiffrin, 1968), information passes through the stores in which order?
options: short-term memory, sensory register, long-term memory
sensory register, long-term memory, short-term memory
long-term memory, short-term memory, sensory register
sensory register, short-term memory, long-term memory
questions.explanation: Information first enters the sensory register, attended information is transferred to short-term memory, and rehearsed or encoded information is transferred to long-term memory. Retrieval brings it back from long-term memory into short-term memory.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares iconic and echoic memory?
options: Both last about 18 to 30 seconds without rehearsal
Both have a capacity of about seven items
Echoic memory lasts several seconds, longer than iconic memory
Iconic memory lasts several seconds, longer than echoic memory
questions.explanation: Iconic memory lasts only a fraction of a second, while echoic memory lasts about three to four seconds. The 18 to 30 second duration and the capacity of about seven items describe short-term memory.

questions.stem: The capacity of short-term memory is usually described as:
options: a single item at a time
about seven items, plus or minus two
about 20 items, plus or minus five
unlimited, but only for a short time
questions.explanation: Short-term memory has a limited capacity of about five to nine items. When it is full, new information pushes old information out. Unlimited capacity describes long-term memory.

questions.stem: Information in short-term memory is mainly encoded ____, while information in long-term memory is mainly encoded ____.
questions.explanation: Short-term memory mainly encodes information by its sound, which is why acoustically similar items are easily confused. Long-term memory mainly encodes information by its meaning.

questions.stem: A participant briefly sees a list and later writes BOAT instead of COAT. In a separate test weeks later, she confuses HUGE with LARGE. These errors suggest:
options: visual encoding in both STM and LTM
acoustic encoding in both STM and LTM
acoustic encoding in STM and semantic encoding in LTM
semantic encoding in STM and acoustic encoding in LTM
questions.explanation: Confusing words that sound alike soon after seeing them points to acoustic encoding in short-term memory. Confusing words with similar meanings after a long delay points to semantic encoding in long-term memory.

questions.stem: Memory for how to ride a bike, which is shown through performance rather than conscious recall, is:
questions.explanation: Procedural memory is implicit memory for skills and actions, retrieved without conscious awareness. Semantic and episodic memories are explicit, so they are consciously recalled.

questions.stem: Lena remembers that Perth is the capital of Western Australia but not when she learned it. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Semantic memory holds general facts and knowledge not tied to a personal experience. Episodic memory would include where and when a personal event happened.

questions.stem: Which is an example of episodic memory?
options: Knowing that a birthday is celebrated once a year
Being able to light birthday candles without thinking
Holding a phone number in mind for a few seconds
Remembering what you did at your last birthday party
questions.explanation: Episodic memory is explicit memory for personally experienced events, including their time and place. A general fact about birthdays is semantic, and a practised action is procedural.

questions.stem: In the working memory model, which component controls attention and coordinates the other components?
questions.explanation: The central executive directs attention and coordinates the slave systems. The phonological loop holds sound-based information and the visuospatial sketchpad holds visual and spatial information.

questions.stem: While driving, Jo mentally pictures the route to a friend's house. Which component of working memory is she mainly using?
questions.explanation: The visuospatial sketchpad holds and manipulates visual and spatial information such as routes and layouts. The phonological loop handles verbal and sound-based information.

questions.stem: The episodic buffer was added to the working memory model in 2000. Its role is to:
options: integrate information from the other components and long-term memory
rehearse verbal information by silently repeating it
hold raw visual information for a fraction of a second
permanently store personal memories of life events
questions.explanation: Baddeley added the episodic buffer to explain how information from the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad and long-term memory is combined into single episodes. It is a temporary store, not a permanent one.

questions.stem: A student finds it easy to listen to music while drawing a diagram but hard to read notes while listening to a podcast. The working memory model explains this because:
options: the episodic buffer cannot hold more than one task
the central executive stores verbal information
two verbal tasks compete for the phonological loop
two visual tasks compete for the visuospatial sketchpad
questions.explanation: Reading and listening to speech both draw on the phonological loop, so the tasks interfere. Music and drawing use different components, so they can be done together more easily.

questions.stem: How does the working memory model differ from the multi-store model's view of short-term memory?
options: It says short-term memory has unlimited capacity
It treats short-term memory as several active components
It treats short-term memory as a single passive store
It removes short-term memory and keeps only long-term memory
questions.explanation: The multi-store model describes short-term memory as a single store. The working memory model breaks it into a central executive and separate systems that actively process information, which better explains doing two different tasks at once.

questions.stem: Which brain structure plays a key role in forming explicit memories and transferring them to long-term storage?
questions.explanation: The hippocampus consolidates new explicit (semantic and episodic) memories and helps transfer them to long-term storage in the cortex. The cerebellum is mainly involved in implicit procedural memories.

questions.stem: After surgery in 1953 that removed much of the hippocampus on both sides, Henry Molaison:
options: lost his short-term memory but kept all long-term memory
could not form new explicit memories but could learn new motor skills
could form new explicit memories but lost all motor skills
lost all memories from before the surgery but learned new facts normally
questions.explanation: Henry Molaison had severe anterograde amnesia for new facts and events, but he improved at a mirror-drawing task without remembering doing it. His short-term memory and many older memories were largely intact.

questions.stem: Henry Molaison improved at mirror drawing over several days while saying each time that he had never done the task. This suggests that:
options: implicit memories do not depend on the hippocampus
explicit memories are stored in the cerebellum
questions.explanation: His skill improved, so procedural memory was being formed by structures such as the cerebellum. He could not consciously recall practising, which shows explicit memory formation depends on the hippocampus.

questions.stem: Which brain structure is mainly involved in forming and storing implicit memories such as a tennis serve?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum is involved in the formation and storage of implicit procedural memories for skilled, coordinated movements. The hippocampus is involved in explicit memories.

questions.stem: A person vividly remembers a car accident and feels fear whenever she hears screeching tyres. Which structure most strongly contributed to the emotional part of this memory?
questions.explanation: The amygdala attaches emotional significance, especially fear, to memories and strengthens the formation of emotionally arousing memories. The hippocampus helps form the explicit facts of the event.

questions.stem: Writing down as many items as you can remember from a shopping list, in any order, is an example of:
questions.explanation: Free recall means retrieving information in any order with no cues. Serial recall requires the original order, and cued recall gives prompts to help retrieval.

questions.stem: A student is asked to name the planets in their order from the Sun. This is:
questions.explanation: Serial recall requires information to be retrieved in the order in which it was learned. Free recall allows any order.

questions.stem: A multiple-choice test question mainly tests retrieval by:
questions.explanation: Recognition involves identifying the correct information from options presented. It is usually easier than recall because the options act as strong retrieval cues.

questions.stem: Ali took 20 trials to learn a list and, a month later, took 5 trials to relearn it. His savings score is:
questions.explanation: Savings = (original trials - relearning trials) / original trials x 100 = (20 - 5) / 20 x 100 = 75%. A score of 25% comes from dividing the relearning trials by the original trials.

questions.stem: Relearning is considered the most sensitive measure of retention because it:
options: requires the information to be retrieved in order
provides strong cues such as the first letter of each word
tests only memories stored in the sensory register
can show retention when recall and recognition show none
questions.explanation: Information that cannot be recalled or recognised is often relearned faster than it was first learned. That saving shows some information was retained, which the other measures miss.

questions.stem: According to the levels of processing model (Craik and Lockhart, 1972), which type of processing leads to the best retention?
questions.explanation: The model proposes that deeper processing, which focuses on meaning, produces a more durable memory. Structural (appearance) and phonemic (sound) processing are shallow.

questions.stem: Asking 'Does the word rhyme with WEIGHT?' requires which level of processing?
questions.explanation: Judging rhyme requires attention to the sound of the word, which is phonemic processing. It is shallower than semantic processing, which attends to meaning.

questions.stem: In Craik and Tulving's (1975) experiment two, participants answered questions about 60 words and were then unexpectedly given a list of 180 words. What were they asked to do?
options: tick the words they had seen in the first phase
write down all the words they could remember
recall the words in their original order
relearn the list until they could recall all 60
questions.explanation: The retention test in experiment two was a recognition test: 180 words, the 60 originals plus 120 distractors, and participants checked the ones they had seen. Participants had not been told there would be a memory test.

questions.stem: In Craik and Tulving's (1975) experiment two, recognition of 'yes' words rose from about 15% for case questions to about 81% for sentence questions. The best conclusion is that:
options: longer exposure to the words caused the higher recognition
intentional learning was better than incidental learning
semantic processing produced better retention than structural processing
phonemic processing produced better retention than semantic processing
questions.explanation: Each word was shown for the same 200 milliseconds, so the difference came from the type of question asked. Sentence questions required processing meaning, which produced far higher recognition than judging the case of the letters.

questions.stem: A criticism of the levels of processing model is that:
options: it was supported only by case studies of brain injury
it claims short-term memory has unlimited capacity
depth is hard to measure independently of how well items are remembered
it cannot explain why rhyming words are remembered at all
questions.explanation: If a well-remembered item is simply assumed to have been deeply processed, the argument is circular. Craik and Tulving tried to address this by using decision time as an index of depth.

questions.stem: Repeating information over and over to keep it in short-term memory is called:
questions.explanation: Maintenance rehearsal is simple repetition that keeps information active in short-term memory. Elaborative rehearsal links new information to existing knowledge and meaning.

questions.stem: To learn the term 'myelin', Priya links it to how insulation on an electrical cord speeds up a signal. This strategy is:
questions.explanation: Elaborative rehearsal connects new information with meaningful information already in long-term memory. It involves deeper processing than repetition, so it produces better long-term retention.

questions.stem: Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve (1885) shows that forgetting is:
options: rapid soon after learning, then slows and levels off
slow at first, then becomes rapid after several days
steady at the same rate for weeks after learning
absent for the first day, then complete within a week
questions.explanation: Ebbinghaus found the greatest loss occurred within the first hour or so after learning, after which the rate of forgetting slowed. Some information was retained even after long delays.

questions.stem: Ebbinghaus used nonsense syllables such as 'DAX' and tested only himself. Which is the best evaluation of this method?
options: Testing himself made the results generalisable to all people
Nonsense syllables are processed semantically, which improved recall
Using one participant removed every extraneous variable
Meaningless syllables reduced prior knowledge but limit generalisability
questions.explanation: Nonsense syllables meant his existing knowledge could not help, but memory for meaningless material in one person may not apply to meaningful material in others. A sample of one cannot represent a population.

questions.stem: Ebbinghaus found that the more times he repeated a list, the fewer trials he needed to relearn it later. This shows that:
options: repetition causes faster decay of the memory trace
repetition replaces the need for retrieval cues
repetition increases the savings shown on relearning
questions.explanation: Greater repetition at learning produced greater savings when the list was relearned, showing more information had been retained. This supports repetition as a strategy to improve memory.
